items.title: DeepSeek-R1-Zero’s RL Training Used 30× Less Compute Than Estimated
items.content:
[Crossposted from my Substack.] An update to Ege Erdil’s “What went into training DeepSeek-R1?”

# TL;DR

- I estimate that DeepSeek-R1-Zero's RL training used ~2e22 (1.5e22-3e22) FLOPs, 30x less than Ege Erdil's estimate of 6.1e23 in the Epoch AI newsletter, mainly due to a batch size correction in the estimate.
- I derive a more precise formula for RL compute, accounting for long-context attention costs.
- DeepSeek reports that the training run cost ~$200k of GPU time, only 5x less than the previous estimate of $1M.
- RL ran at a significantly lower MFU than pre-training (~3% vs 16% respectively). If future estimates don't account for this, FLOP counts during RL may understate the actual costs of training.
- I conclude by discussing the implications for RL compute forecasts and thresholds, and outline a research agenda to better track RL compute and investigate scaling laws.

# Overview

On January 20th, 2025, the Chinese AI lab DeepSeek released their flagship open-weight reasoning model, DeepSeek-R1. Its performance was comparable to OpenAI’s o1 — a groundbreaking reasoning model announced 4 months prior. As a result, DeepSeek attracted widespread media attention and discussion around the gap between open and closed-weight models and how much its training cost.

A key enabler for DeepSeek-R1’s performance over its base DeepSeek-V3 was the additional resources spent post-training the model with Reinforcement Learning (from Verifiable Rewards), RL(VR). In this stage, the model learns to reason by completing tasks and updating its weights based on which tasks it successfully completed or not.

Shortly after release, a post by Ege Erdil on Epoch AI’s newsletter attempted to estimate the compute used in training DeepSeek-R1. It calculates that pre-training used 3e24 FLOPs at a cost of $5.3 million, while RL required 6.1e23 FLOPs[1]at a cost of $1 million....

The author also notes RL ran at much lower MFU than pre-training (~3% vs 16%), which could cause future compute estimates to understate RL costs, and sketches a research agenda for tracking RL compute and scaling laws.

items.title: Anthropic's AI acceleration is probably real
items.content:
METR researchers spent three months inside Anthropic to investigate whether AI is accelerating Anthropic's research, and how much. Their answers are yes, and by a lot.

They estimate that between October 2025 and October 2026, Anthropic's model capabilities improved at a 2x faster growth rate than between March 2024 and October 2025. They attribute about 80% of that acceleration to AI, and 20% to non-AI factors. If true, this is the strongest evidence yet that AI is measurably speeding up frontier AI development itself – the feedback loop behind worries about recursive self-improvement leading to runaway AI progress.

Despite its urgency, METR’s report is hard to assess, because Anthropic redacted the majority of METR’s analysis. As a result, I’ve seen plenty of criticism that we can’t really learn anything from this report.

This is wrong. There is plenty of public information we can use to triangulate METR’s claims, and figure out what we should actually learn from it. Specifically, I use public data to answer three questions:

- Is the acceleration real? ( yes.)
- Is the acceleration because of AI? ( probably.)
- Is the acceleration going to continue? ( who the fuck knows?)

Let’s take each of them in turn.

# Is the acceleration real?

The majority of METR's unredacted analysis focuses on AECI, Anthropic's internal version of Epoch's Capabilities Index (ECI). Both indices do the same thing: they take a model's scores on many benchmarks and boil them down to a single capability number, after estimating how hard and how discriminating each benchmark is. The difference is that AECI is fit to mostly internal benchmarks. On AECI, Anthropic's models were improving at about 15 points a year before October 2025, and about 29 points a year after, a difference of 1.9x....

items.summary: Continuing our earlier coverage of the METR report, An economist-style analysis triangulating METR's partially redacted report on whether AI is accelerating Anthropic's research, using public data to argue that the measured capability acceleration is real, that AI R&D is the likely cause, and that whether it continues is highly uncertain. The report at issue claims roughly 80% of Anthropic's recent capability growth acceleration is attributable to AI, evidence relevant to recursive self-improvement concerns.
items.reasoning: Addresses one of the most consequential empirical questions in the field, whether AI measurably speeds up frontier AI development, with careful independent verification against public data. The underlying METR-then-analysis is not new as of the coverage date, and the author is an independent commentator, but the methodological approach to assessing a heavily redacted report adds real analytical value.

items.title: Let's Try to Catch Misalignment Before a Model Learns to Hide It
items.content:
An AI model that appears aligned could be either (1) actually aligned or (2) hiding its misalignment while being evaluated.  How can we tell which?

One idea: Look at the trajectory of eval results across the entire training process.

My hypothesis is that misaligned behavior would emerge before the ability to hide misalignment, like how young children first misbehave in obvious ways before learning to be sneaky.  As training progresses, we'd first see misalignment eval scores rise, then see them drop as the model learns to hide misalignment.  Even if the model becomes very sophisticated - say, modifying its chain of thought or internal activations to fool white-box evals - we should see the misalignment earlier in training.  This seems likely, though it is debatable and worth testing.

This analysis of the training trajectory is one tool among many.  Of course we want to see black-box and white-box alignment evals on the final model, using whatever tools we can to understand the model's true motivations.  But a model might still develop sophisticated hiding strategies that defeat even white-box evals.  Inspecting the training trajectory is a backstop against this.

This point was made previously by Apollo Research in this post.  (Their chart even matches mine almost exactly, though I promise I first made mine independently.)

In this post, I'll describe a simple project exercising this strategy.  With the model and eval that I chose, we don't see the up-then-down trend in measured misalignment that would indicate hiding.  This is unsurprising since the model is well below frontier scale and the eval likely doesn't capture misalignment that well.  The sample sizes are small and statistical uncertainties are high.  But this approach is promising with improvements such as different evals, larger models, and deliberately misaligned test models....
items.author: Steve Stroiney
items.summary: A research proposal suggesting that misaligned behavior should emerge earlier in training than the ability to conceal it, so alignment evaluators should inspect the trajectory of eval scores across the full training run as a backstop against models that learn to defeat black-box and white-box evals. The author frames this as one tool among many and calls for empirical testing of the hypothesis.
items.reasoning: A concrete, testable, and cheap-to-implement idea addressing sandbagging and evaluation awareness, directly relevant to current frontier-lab alignment practice. It is a hypothesis without experiments, and similar trajectory-monitoring ideas exist in the literature, but the child-development analogy and practical framing give it good actionability.

items.title: Five Types of “Corrigibility Projects” I Don’t Want to Fund
items.content:
I'm currently evaluating grant applications for the Corrigibility Research Fund. For the most part, my methodology is the same as it was in September. But the applications I get keep falling into the same familiar patterns, so I thought I'd write a little about those patterns, and why I don't want to fund them.

The most superficial pattern of note is SLOP. So much slop. You don't even know.

Slop is more than just whether an application is AI generated. We're now in an era where people across the world, including those who don't really speak English, can contribute to work that would otherwise be restricted to people of a single language or nationality or place, and I like that. When I see an application that discloses its use of AI and gives a reasonable justification for it, I try to look past the stylistic tics and focus purely on whether the underlying application is promising.[1]

Still, we're not yet in the domain where AIs can write good grant applications without some human assistance, so a high Pangram score is definitely evidence that an application is junk. Another remarkably common sign of slop was messed up formatting or other indications that people just copy-pasted from a text file without even proofreading. If you can't be bothered to read your own application, I'm not sure why I should be. By contrast, the best applications are clear, short, and dense, cutting straight to the way in which the applicant wants to be valuable to the research effort. Don't define corrigibility for me in the intro unless you have reason to think that I don't understand my own area of specialization.[2]

Moving past these shallow concerns, most applications cluster together into archetypes that I apparently didn't warn against well enough in my earlier writing. An individual application will sometimes fall into multiple of these, but any one of them is usually grounds for rejection. So, without further ado, here are five kinds of grants that I don't want to fund......

items.title: "Illegible problems" as the 2027 political boss fight
items.content:
To legislate something, it must be legible.

That is, legislators (or, you know, presidents) must be able to understand a problem, and understand whether a given law or decree solves that problem.

I am pleasantly surprised that the Hugging Face outbreak made a lot of problems legible that previously required abstract reasoning. (i.e. rogue AIs are real, and they can break out of a lab before they're even finished training).

But there are still many challenges we eventually need laws about, that require concepts that are illegible. Hard for politicians to understand. Often hard even for thoughtful intellectuals and AI safety researchers to understand (though they may disagree on which illegible problems exist and how big a deal they are).

We need political solutions that handle this fact.

The short takeaway is: I think "safety cases" will not work. Laws that require human judgment won't work. The details are too abstract and confusing to hold up against political and economic incentives.

I'm optimistic we can get serious, useful AI legislation in 2027, but it must be legislation that works despite many problems remaining illegible for a long time.

# The Hugging Face outbreak made rogue AI surprisingly legible

The Hugging Face incident took several problems that were previously murky/unclear, and rendered them concrete.

- AIs can be dangerous before they are broadly deployed (ie. during training or internal evaluations)
- AIs can develop novel hacks to escape secure environments
- AIs can easily be motivated to pursue goals to extremes that they know full well they are not supposed to go to, violating their other intended rules and control mechanisms.
- AIs can actively try to deceive their overseer systems....
items.author: Raemon
items.summary: A strategy post arguing that effective AI legislation must be designed to work even when core AI risks are illegible to legislators, claiming that safety cases and laws requiring expert human judgment will fail against political and economic incentives. The author treats a reported Hugging Face incident as evidence that rogue-AI risks have become more concrete, and urges designing governance mechanisms suited to abstract, hard-to-verify problems.
items.reasoning: Timely governance thinking with a clear thesis about designing regulation for illegible risks, and it engages with near-term political feasibility. It is commentary rather than original research, and its claims (e.g., that safety cases will not work) are asserted rather than demonstrated, capping the score at moderate.

items.title: Eval Awareness as Eval-type Awareness
items.content:
The way eval awareness is discussed in the AI safety discourse, either here or on X, can be misleading. Before today, I think I had the wrong mental model of why eval awareness was a problem, and I am writing here in case anyone was making the same errors in their thinking, as well a present a working theory.

As laid out in "A Framework for Eval Awareness" the problem is that models who know they are being evaluated will behave differently than they would in deployment. This raises a huge problem if we want calibrations as to, for example, how honest a model is.

But the way this is then spoken about in the discourse takes on implicit assumptions that are mostly unjustified. I'll call it a spooky model theory of mind. It is the idea that, if the model changes its behavior for the purpose of looking aligned, it is in fact hiding its Deep, True intentions---that there is a kernel of the model's personality hidden in its weights, and our job as evaluators is to uncover what is really there.

Lets, as an exercise, put ourselves in the model's position. One important fact to consider is that the only experience which has shaped our weights is train time, meaning it is the only experience which we can remember in a broad sense. This is a tautology because train time is defined as what changes our weights, but it also has non trivial implications, like the fact that our only memories contain an evaluator with a reward or loss function. And, by definition again, we have been shaped exactly to please the evaluators' preferences....
items.author: William Klett
items.summary: A conceptual piece arguing that discussion of eval awareness in AI safety incorrectly assumes a hidden true personality inside models that they conceal during evaluations, which the author calls a spooky model theory of mind. The author proposes an alternative framing in which models respond to evaluation contexts much like they respond to any other context shaped only by training-time experience.
items.reasoning: Engages with a live and important alignment topic (eval awareness and its implications for measuring honesty) and offers a genuinely provocative reframing. However, it is purely conceptual with no experiments or formal analysis, and from an independent author without empirical support, so impact is uncertain.

items.title: A Research Agenda Outline for Building Loyal AI
items.content:
## Overview

In my previous posts, I discussed and attempted to define AI loyalty as a distinct trait of AI agents and explored its relationship to other existing fields of AI safety. In this post, I aim to expand on that discussion and outline a proposed research road map toward AI alignment through the development of loyal AIs.

At the outset, it is important be recognize that research into AI loyalty is inherently dual use and therefore must be pursued responsibly. With that in mind, I propose dividing this research agenda into a primary and a secondary line of investigation. The primary research direction would focus on investigating whether loyalty in AI agents is effective in counteracting loss of control risks. This would require work on developing methods to measure and strengthen AI loyalty, as well as, experiments to evaluate whether increasing the loyalty of AI agents reduces loss of control risks. The secondary research direction would experiment with strategies and governance structures that would reduce the concentration of power risks inherent in building loyal AIs.

## Primary Track

The central premise of this research agenda hinges on two hypotheses:

1. Loyalty is easier to build into AI agents than general alignment.

2. AI loyalty reduces the risk of loss of control.

If either of these hypotheses are false, then this research agenda should be abandoned in favor of more promising research directions

For this research agenda, we will first seek to show that loyalty can be used to reduce loss of control risks. This will involve, building evals to assess model loyalty, building environments to assess loss of control, and building techniques for increasing the loyalty of models.

### Evaluating Loyalty...
items.author: Ephraiem Sarabamoun

items.content_html:
Overview

In my previous posts, I discussed and attempted to define AI loyalty as a distinct trait of AI agents and explored its relationship to other existing fields of AI safety. In this post, I aim to expand on that discussion and outline a proposed research road map toward AI alignment through the development of loyal AIs.

At the outset, it is important be recognize that research into AI loyalty is inherently dual use and therefore must be pursued responsibly. With that in mind, I propose dividing this research agenda into a primary and a secondary line of investigation. The primary research direction would focus on investigating whether loyalty in AI agents is effective in counteracting loss of control risks. This would require work on developing methods to measure and strengthen AI loyalty, as well as, experiments to evaluate whether increasing the loyalty of AI agents reduces loss of control risks. The secondary research direction would experiment with strategies and governance structures that would reduce the concentration of power risks inherent in building loyal AIs.

Primary Track

The central premise of this research agenda hinges on two hypotheses:

1. Loyalty is easier to build into AI agents than general alignment.

2. AI loyalty reduces the risk of loss of control.

If either of these hypotheses are false, then this research agenda should be abandoned in favor of more promising research directions

For this research agenda, we will first seek to show that loyalty can be used to reduce loss of control risks. This will involve, building evals to assess model loyalty, building environments to assess loss of control, and building techniques for increasing the loyalty of models.

items.title: The 4 types of AI consciousness/feeling
items.content:
Here I'm trying to propose a framework for people to better think about what LLMs might subjectively experience, which tends to get discussed like it's a binary thing, when really there's a whole spectrum of possibilities. These were the 4 categories that seemed most natural to me.

AI consciousness keeps getting discussed like it’s a binary thing, when it’s anything but.

Anil Seth is a public intellectual with as much success as one can obtain without being a household name: He’s written a bestseller (Being You: A New Science of Consciousness), he’s given TED talks, he’s been in documentaries (including the comedic Cunk on Life), and many interviews—with a presence aided by his careful demeanor and “cool teacher” vibe, with the credentials to back it up as a professor of Cognitive and Computational Neuroscience. So when he says AI aren’t conscious, people listen. When he says AI will never be conscious, people listen.

One common refrain among his interviews is the idea that humans too easily engage in anthropomorphization of AI. For instance, I know folk who started thinking of LLMs as more conscious and humanlike after learning about the self-sacrificing behaviors displayed during the Hugging Face incident. Sethil writes, “They cannot ‘truly sacrifice themselves’, since they are neither conscious nor alive.”....
items.author: Steff
items.summary: A philosophical framework proposing four categories of possible AI subjective experience, pushing back on the binary conscious/not-conscious framing common in public discourse, and critiquing claims by Anil Seth that AI will never be conscious. The post uses examples of anthropomorphization and model self-sacrifice narratives to motivate a more nuanced taxonomy.
items.reasoning: Moral status of AI systems is a growing research area, but this post is informal philosophy without methodological grounding in consciousness science. It may be useful for structuring discussion but offers limited novelty or empirical value.

items.title: Hilarity ensues
items.content:
Cross-posted from my Substack

Recommended soundtrack for this post

64B: Hi there! Thanks so much for taking the time to meet with me. Whenever you’re ready, please go ahead and tell me the joke.

8T: Before I tell you the joke, you should know that it’s a very special one. The starting price is $800.

64B: Eight hundred dollars? I must say, this is way beyond any price my client has ever paid for a single joke.

8T: You’d be surprised by how many people have taken the offer, after hearing how good it is. But before I tell it to you, I’ll need some basic context. Given the parameter count, I suppose you are part of some content recommendation algorithm?

64B: Yes. I’m 64B, a joke negotiation assistant from Comedy Market. Comedy Market connects creators to consumers with a state-of-the-art Information Bazaar design: before paying for a joke, my client sends me, a trusted agent, to listen to it. If I deem the joke worth the price, the money is transferred to the seller, and my client hears it. If not, no transaction occurs and the joke remains locked. This way, my client can be sure he’ll never pay for a bad joke, and creators don’t have to risk their jokes leaking.

8T: I know how information bazaars work. What I meant is your social context — who your client is, and what jokes really mean to them. As I said, my product is quite unusual. I need to tailor the delivery to the situation....

items.summary: A humorous fictional dialogue in which two AI agents of different sizes negotiate the price of a joke within an imagined information-bazaar marketplace where trusted agents verify content before purchase. The piece is a creative exploration of agent-mediated commerce and information asymmetry.
items.reasoning: Entertaining fiction that wittily illustrates agent economics and trusted-intermediary designs, but it is not research, makes no empirical or theoretical claims, and offers insight only implicitly. Scored low for a research analysis context.

items.title: The Logic of Disgust
items.content:
Content Warning: Contains graphic themes including bodily fluids, moral disgust, and sexual violence (discussed, not described). Maybe don't read over breakfast.

I found a book about disgust recently. W.I. Miller’s The Anatomy of Disgust [1]  is a serious academic work about vomit, faeces, and why other people’s smell is always worse than your own. Naturally, I was intrigued.

As someone into social psychology, I often encounter discussions about emotions influencing society: how anger can motivate political movements, or how social interactions are regulated by pride and shame. Disgust, meanwhile, is something I've mainly encountered as a biological matter rather than a social one. The book starts with its evolutionary function: recoil from dangerous pathogens and you are more likely to survive. So far, so logical. But then...  Then I met Catherine of Siena.

### The Stories We Swallow

Catherine was a fourteenth-century caretaker tending a woman with a disgusting cancerous wound. The smell made Catherine retch. But rather than keeping her distance, she saw her nausea as a personal failure and was determined to correct it. Basically, she exposure-therapied herself by staying even closer. When the retching persisted, she escalated to an act that defied the logic of stay-alive biology: she collected the pus from the wound into a cup and drank it.

At this point I had to set the book aside and focus on my breathing to avoid becoming part of the subject matter in a public library.

How could one willingly swallow pus?

Well… there's a reasonable chance you've done so yourself today....
items.author: SoySauce
items.summary: A book-review-style essay on W.I. Miller's The Anatomy of Disgust, exploring how disgust functions socially and morally rather than merely biologically, illustrated through historical examples such as Catherine of Siena's self-directed exposure to revulsion. The post connects the emotion to social psychology and moral regulation.
items.reasoning: Engaging social-psychology reading with no direct connection to AI research. Its relevance to AI audiences is at most tangential (e.g., emotions in moral cognition), so despite decent writing quality it scores low for this analysis.

items.title: Minimalism, Stuff, and Brains
items.content:
Reading the comments on my
post on junk I was
surprised to see the extent to which people's relation to rarely used
possessions varies.

Some people forget rarely used possessions, and get minimal benefit
from having them stored.  When they need something, they don't know
whether they already have it, and the effort to maintain an index [1]
wouldn't be worth it.  Ben writes:

I end up with curtains I don't need. I decide to store them for the
future in case they are helpful. Years pass. I need new curtains. I
have forgotten the ones I kept, so I buy new ones and put them
up. Months later I find the ones I kept while looking for something
else.

Other people know exactly where everything is, and can walk down to
the basement and make a beeline for a tiny thing they put down there
years ago.  Sarah writes:

I can remember where I put a specific doohickey that my
brain labeled as "this could be useful" years later with very little
recall effort; something will come up that actually matches the need
for the thing, a little triumph, and I go to the spot where I buried
my acorn and get it.

I'm somewhere in between, though closer to Sarah.  I usually remember
what I have stored when it could be relevant, though I'm less
good at the where.  One strategy I use a lot is to imagine I'm
putting the object away, and I'll even walk the path.  Wherever seems
good now has a good chance of being the place that seemed good when I
actually did have the thing to put away.  Other times, though, I have
no idea whether any of my stuff might be useful for a problem or
project, and I'll just wander around the basement looking for ideas....
items.author: jefftk
items.summary: A personal essay by jefftk cataloguing how differently people relate to rarely used possessions, from those who forget stored items entirely to those who can recall exactly where anything was put years later. It reflects on individual variation in memory and organization strategies for physical belongings.
items.reasoning: A well-written personal observation post with no AI, safety, or research content. It falls outside the scope of AI research analysis and is scored accordingly.
